summary: Explores the issues behind host firewalls, which run on end-user systems, and notes that software is often running while its communication is blocked. It suggests ways to improve the architecture going forward.

plainLanguage.summary: A firewall on your own computer sometimes blocks a program that is running anyway. This asks if we could be smarter, like not starting the program at all.

subtitle: Why software gets firewalled instead of fixed, updated, or stopped

tldr.problem: Host firewalls on user computers often run software in a restricted state where communication is blocked, even though the software consumes resources. This treats the symptom (unwanted communication) rather than the root causes (buggy software, outdated software, or software the user doesn't want).
tldr.mechanism: The RFC categorizes firewall rules into two types: preventing unintended application behavior, and enforcing administrator policy. For each category, it describes three possible approaches (fix the software, don't use the software, or firewall it) and evaluates the trade-offs and architectural implications.
tldr.outcome: Better application awareness of network constraints, stronger automatic update mechanisms, and host firewall designs that require explicit application consent would reduce the need for behind-the-firewall execution.

facts.label: Approaches to unwanted behavior
facts.value: 3 (fix software, don't use it, firewall it)

today: RFC 7288 is an Informational RFC from the Internet Architecture Board that remains active. It represents the IAB's reflection on architectural issues with host firewalls and continues to inform discussions about system design and the trade-offs inherent in blocking versus preventing unwanted application behavior.

sections.title: The Host Firewall Problem
sections.content:
A host firewall runs on an individual user's computer, unlike a network firewall which protects a whole network. Today's approach is that software may run and consume memory, CPU, and bandwidth, but a host firewall blocks its communication. The RFC questions whether this end state is actually desirable or just the best achievable today, and whether it makes architectural sense.

The RFC defines "firewall" informally as "something that blocks unwanted traffic," but the critical question is: unwanted by whom? A single piece of traffic might be wanted by the end user but unwanted by the administrator, or wanted by the developer but unwanted by both. Different entities (end users, application developers, network administrators, host administrators, firewall vendors) have conflicting desires, which means there are multiple types of firewalls and architectural trade-offs inherent in the design.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall on your computer blocks stuff, but who decides what's bad: you, your app maker, your boss, or the security company? They all want different things.

sections.title: Two Categories of Firewall Rules
sections.content:
Firewall rules fall into two fundamental categories. The first is attack surface reduction: rules intended to prevent applications from doing things the developer did not want them to do. This includes preventing exploitation of bugs or vulnerabilities, and providing 'stealth mode' so the host doesn't respond to port scans. The second category is security policy: rules that prevent applications from doing things the developer might have intended, but which an administrator or user policy forbids.

For attack surface reduction, developers might not want a firewall at all if they fix bugs promptly and automatically. For security policy, there is genuine tension: administrators want centralized control, while applications want to make their own decisions or require explicit consent from users.
sections.plainLanguage: Some rules stop the program from doing something the maker didn't intend. Other rules stop the program from doing something the maker did intend but your boss doesn't want.

sections.title: Three Approaches to Unwanted Behavior
sections.content:
When running an application would cause unwanted behavior, customers have three choices. First, fix the software: most modern operating systems and many applications now have automatic updates, but not all, and some environments require testing and recertification before updates can be deployed. Second, don't use the software: if the software can still do something useful when firewalled (like playing single-player mode when multi-player is blocked), this is unrealistic. Third, let the software run behind a host firewall: this has significant downsides including resource consumption, poor user experience (the user doesn't know why the app doesn't work), and firewall rules that block more than intended, interfering with protocol operation and innovation.

The RFC argues that mechanisms for encouraging secure automatic software updates are important and would greatly reduce overall complexity. Additionally, applications should be more aware of their environment constraints so they can fail gracefully when firewalled.
sections.plainLanguage: You can fix the program, stop using it, or let it run but blocked. Each has problems, so the better answer is for programs to update automatically and know when they're blocked.

sections.title: Where to Enforce Policy
sections.content: For security policy enforcement, the RFC compares three options. First, policies in applications: each app implements support for complex policies. This is impractical because the complexity is error-prone and inconsistent across hundreds of applications. Second, policies in host firewalls: this avoids explicit application interaction but creates 'arms races' where applications re-engineer protocols to bypass filters (using HTTP as transport when firewalls allow it but drop unknown protocols). Third, policies in a service or library: the application explicitly requests network access and a library or OS service mediates it, giving the application visibility into policy constraints. This approach, used by some OS firewalls and by PCP (Port Control Protocol), lessens arms races and gives better user experience. However, there is no standard mechanism today for a library or service to learn complex policies from the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Policy can live in the app (complex), the firewall (creates arms races), or a shared library (better but needs standards).

sections.title: Special Case: Stealth Mode
sections.content: A special case arises from the desire to hide from address and port scans on public networks. RFC compliance requires responding to certain messages: TCP compliance requires sending RST in response to a SYN when there is no listener, and ICMPv6 compliance requires sending Echo Reply to Echo Request. A firewall can drop these outbound messages after the application generates them, creating 'stealth' without violating the RFCs. However, fewer resources would be consumed if the application never generated the message in the first place. This is another case where application awareness of its environment would be preferable to firewall blocking.
sections.plainLanguage: To hide from port scans, a firewall can drop the responses your computer would normally send. But it's more efficient if your computer knows not to send them at all.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content: The RFC concludes with a note that there is a common misconception that firewalls protect users from malware, when in fact they protect users from buggy software. Host firewalls give users a false sense of security because they are not invulnerable and will not prevent malware if the user allows it to run. The RFC's broader point is architectural: today's host firewall deployments represent a compromise where running-but-blocked software is accepted as inevitable. Better system design would eliminate this compromise through automatic updates, application awareness of network constraints, and policy enforcement mechanisms that do not require running software with restricted communication.
sections.plainLanguage: Firewalls help with bugs, not malware. The real answer is better programs that update themselves and know when they can't connect.
